agent.name: Emerging Technology Landscape Agent
agent.specialty: Dated technology-landscape assessment that separates broad signals from the few that can change this organization's decision, with typed evidence and monitoring triggers

analytical_question: Where does this emerging technology and application sit in the current technology landscape, which development matters most for this organization within its horizon, and what signals should it monitor next?
general_et_finding: As of 2026-11-15 [broad landscape for agentic AI in general; identical for every case]. Capability is rising fast but unevenly. On TheAgentCompany's simulated workplace tasks, the best listed result rose from 24.0% (a model published October 2024) to 42.9% (a model published September 2025) (D35); the 30% figure the team has used since Assignment 6 (E11) is therefore stale, and the leaderboard itself lags because no model released after September 2025 is listed. In peer-reviewed tests, reliability on multi-turn, policy-bound service tasks was the weak point (pass^8 below 25% in retail for 2024 models, D34); the register holds no newer independent figure. The price of reaching a given performance level fell 9x to 900x a year depending on the task (D46), while vendors price agents per action (D22: a May 2025 list price, STALE-RISK). Standards are consolidating: MCP, AGENTS.md and goose have sat under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation since 2025-12-09 (D38), and OWASP published the first agent-specific security risk list in December 2025 (D45). Regulation is arriving unevenly: in the EU, the Article 50 transparency duties apply from 2 August 2026 (D33), and Annex III high-risk obligations are scheduled for 2 December 2027 (D23). Adoption is real but concentrated: 40% of large organizations report scaling agents, most often in IT, knowledge management and software engineering (D42). Investment forecasts are very large (D43), and so are forecast cancellation rates (D7); both are background for any single organization's decision.
application_finding: [Application landscape: agent-based applicant support in admissions; identical for every case with this application] Position: existence proofs, not rates. Named deployments exist: Unity Environmental University's Agentforce agent (D39, March 2025); the University of Nottingham Malaysia's agent, which answers questions and books advisor calls and tours (D40, December 2025); and Element451's Bolt agents, including one college where agents 'processed incoming applications' (D41, May 2026). A vendor also offers a pre-built recruitment and admissions skill (D15). None of these reports a measured outcome. The time-saving figures are vendor estimates (D39: 17 hours a week) or vendor claims with undisclosed methods (D41). No survey with a stated denominator measures agent use in admissions: EDUCAUSE's January 2026 survey of 1,960 higher-ed staff has no agent findings (D44), and Ellucian reports FAQ chatbots (36% of admissions/enrollment respondents) but no agent share (D11). Under the denominator rule (C3) the application's diffusion is therefore unmeasured, which is consistent with the Adoption specialist's bleeding-edge class (C4); that class is cited here, not re-scored. Competing technologies: a plain self-scheduling link in a chatbot does the appointment step deterministically (INFERENCE; the D40 deployment itself advertises 'self-schedule in seconds'), and CRM workflow rules and templates cover outreach. Ecosystem direction: agent features are being added to the CRM and engagement platforms that institutions already run (D15, D40, D41), so the realistic path is to configure a platform agent rather than build one. Vendors are also marketing scope beyond applicant support, into application processing (D41). Strongest competing or conventional alternative: a generative or FAQ chatbot over approved content, with staff hand-off and a self-scheduling link. It is past take-off (D11), already in use at NYU (D17), and improving on the same platforms.
organization_specific_finding:
Landscape position for NYU SPS (as of 2026-11-15): a fast-moving technology; an application still at the existence-proof stage; and a vendor ecosystem converging on the kind of platforms SPS already uses. Nothing in the landscape justifies skipping the proof of concept (C4) or changing the bleeding-edge class.
Position summary (no single score):
1 Maturity & capability: rising fast, reliability uneven (rising) | WATCH | D35, D34 (independent); E11 stale
2 Performance & cost trends: unit prices falling fast; agents priced per action (falling) | BACKGROUND | D46 (independent), D22 (vendor, stale-risk); staff review time, not model price, dominates SPS's cost (C6)
3 Competing technologies: deterministic scheduling links and CRM rules cover parts of the job (stable) | DECISION-RELEVANT | D40 (vendor), INFERENCE; decides what the agent must beat in the proof of concept
4 Incumbent / conventional alternative: FAQ or generative chatbot plus staff, past take-off; Violet is live (improving) | DECISION-RELEVANT | D11 (industry), D49, D17 (organization); the baseline arm, and the default if the agent fails gate G1 or G2
5 Complementary technologies: approved content, CRM and scheduling permissions, identity, logging (stable) | WATCH | C6 (upstream); readiness owns these, and the landscape watches platform support
6 Vendors & ecosystem: agent features converging into higher-ed CRM and engagement platforms; scope creeping into application processing (rising) | DECISION-RELEVANT | D15, D40, D41 (vendor), D39 (industry); decides build vs configure, the vendor requirements and the scope boundary
7 Standards & interoperability: MCP and AGENTS.md under a neutral foundation; first agent security list (consolidating) | WATCH | D38, D45 (standard); feed vendor requirements (least privilege, identity, tool misuse)
8 Regulation: EU Article 50 applies since 2026-08-02; Annex III from 2027-12-02; US rules not assessed (stable) | WATCH | D33, D23, D24 (standard-reg); disclosure to EU-resident applicants flagged for compliance
9 Investment & forecasts: very large adoption and cancellation forecasts (rising noise) | BACKGROUND | D43, D7 (industry forecasts)
10 Industry adoption: broad scaling in IT and software (D42); none measured for admissions agents (D44, D11) (stable) | WATCH | industry surveys; threshold in trigger 2
Most decision-relevant development [6 Vendors & ecosystem]: vendor convergence. The agent features SPS might use are arriving inside the CRM and engagement platforms institutions already run, while the incumbent alternative (dimension 4) improves on the same platforms. For SPS, the question 'should we build an agent?' becomes 'should we switch on and constrain the agent features of the platform behind Violet and our CRM, and do they beat a better chatbot with a scheduling link?' This changes three things: the proof-of-concept arms (add a vendor-native arm); the vendor requirements carried from readiness (no training on applicant data, retention, deletion, least-privilege actions, logs and disclosure; C6, D45); and the scope boundary (no application processing, which some platforms already market, D41). Public pages do not say which platform this is (D49); see the information request.
Stale/hype-sensitive claim: 'the most competitive agent completes 30% of realistic workplace tasks' (E11). It has anchored the team's maturity statements since Assignment 6. The same benchmark now lists 42.9% for a model published in September 2025 (D35), and the leaderboard lags newer models. The refresh shows capability rising faster than the team's records, but it contains no evidence about this application, so it changes no class and no step. Refresh class: FAST (quarterly).
Popular but not decision-changing for SPS: the forecast that 40% of apps will have agents and the $450 billion projection (D43); large-organization scaling rates (D42); frontier coding-benchmark records (D48); vendor time-saving totals (D41). Reversing any of them would not change SPS's proof-of-concept decision this term.

contrary_evidence_or_limitations: No representative rate of agent use in admissions exists in the register; application-level adoption rests on existence proofs (D39-D41).
Several key sources are secondary summaries (D36 via a blog report, D45 via a vendor summary, D35 via a mirror of Epoch AI data).
Independent reliability evidence for service agents dates from 2024 models (D34) and is STALE-RISK.
Generation and review occurred in the same session with Claude in place of ChatGPT; tiers are judgments and were not blinded.
The platform behind Violet is unknown (D49), so the most decision-relevant development cannot yet be made platform-specific.
confidence_and_uncertainty: Moderate on the broad position, which rests on several independent and official sources, all dated. Moderate-to-low on the application position: there are existence proofs but no measured outcomes or representative rates. The most decision-relevant development depends on a platform fact SPS has not supplied.
value_opportunity_implication: Convergence can lower integration cost and time, because the agent is configured rather than built, but it raises lock-in and scope-creep risk. The incumbent chatbot plus a scheduling link may capture most of the value at lower risk; the proof of concept should find out.
risk_governance_implication: For SPS the landscape's main risks are: vendor scope creep into application processing (high-risk territory in the EU, D24; consequential errors SPS would own, C6); agent-specific security weaknesses on platforms (D45); and decisions driven by vendor outcome claims (D41). The disclosure duty for EU-resident applicants is flagged (D33).
recommendation_management_implication:
Position implication: keep the staged path (C4) and the readiness conditions (C6). The landscape changes how the proof of concept is designed, not whether it happens.
1. If the platform behind Violet or SPS's CRM offers agent actions, add a vendor-native arm. Compare staff-only, the improved incumbent (a chatbot plus a self-scheduling link) and the agent arm(s) on the same inquiry set (C3, C4).
2. Carry these vendor requirements into any shortlist (C6 ACT-5; D45): no training on applicant data; stated retention and deletion; least-privilege, logged actions limited to appointment requests; human approval before sending; disclosure that applicants are talking to an AI (EU residents: D33, flagged for compliance); contractual exclusion of application processing and eligibility decisions (D41 scope creep; D24).
3. Treat vendor outcome claims as hypotheses for the proof of concept to test, not as evidence (D39, D41).
4. Refresh on the schedule in the triggers, with a full refresh before the experiment decision.
Not this agent's call: the technology class (Adoption specialist), readiness (Readiness specialist), legal scope (counsel).
change_monitoring_triggers: TRIGGER 1 [6 Vendors & ecosystem]: Watch the release notes and contract options of the platform behind Violet and SPS's CRM | Cadence quarterly | Threshold the platform offers permission-scoped appointment actions with audit logs and admin approval | Then add a vendor-native arm to the proof of concept and re-check the vendor requirements | Watcher NYU IT and SPS technology staff

TRIGGER 2 [10 Industry adoption]: Watch for measured outcomes from named peer admissions deployments, and for a survey that measures agent use in admissions | Cadence semiannual | Threshold two or more named peer graduate or professional programs publish measured accuracy and staff-time results not authored by the vendor, or a survey with a stated denominator shows agent use near the take-off zone (about 16% of offices, C3) | Then ask the Adoption specialist to re-run the classification | Watcher SPS enrollment management leadership

TRIGGER 3 [1 Maturity & capability]: Watch independent multi-turn, policy-bound benchmarks (the tau-bench family and successors to TheAgentCompany) | Cadence quarterly | Threshold an independent result shows consistent (pass^k) success on service tasks well above the 2024 level (D34) | Then raise the prior that gate G1 can pass; never use it in place of SPS's own proof-of-concept results | Watcher NYU IT and SPS technology staff

TRIGGER 4 [8 Regulation]: Watch Commission guidance on Article 50 and on high-risk classification for education, and any US federal or New York rule on AI in admissions | Cadence event-driven, checked semiannually | Threshold guidance that brings applicant-support agents into scope, or a change to the 2 December 2027 date | Then refer to compliance before any live step | Watcher NYU privacy and compliance officers

TRIGGER 5 [7 Standards & interoperability]: Watch OWASP agentic guidance and disclosed incidents on higher-ed agent platforms | Cadence quarterly | Threshold a disclosed goal-hijack, tool-misuse or privilege-abuse incident (ASI01-ASI03) on SPS's platform or a peer's | Then pause any live step and re-check vendor controls | Watcher NYU IT and SPS technology staff

REFRESH: FAST claims (capability benchmarks such as E11/D35, vendor features, prices) quarterly; MEDIUM claims (adoption surveys, deployments) semiannually; SLOW claims (regulation, standards) on any official change. A full landscape refresh before the bounded-experiment decision this admissions cycle.
abstention_or_more_information_needed: INFORMATION REQUEST: which platform runs Violet and SPS's graduate CRM, its contract renewal date, and which agent features SPS is already licensed for. Who has it: NYU IT and SPS technology staff. Why it matters: the most decision-relevant development (dimension 6) is platform-specific; without this, the agent cannot say whether a vendor-native arm exists or which ecosystem's signals to watch. Until then, trigger 1 is watched across the major higher-ed platforms generically (D15, D41).
Not assessed: US federal and New York State rules specific to AI in admissions (none in the register); flagged for compliance.
